description: Among this flock of Common Goldeneyes is an unusual female with an entirely orange bill. Normally this feature is used to identify a female Barrow's Goldeneye, but in rare instances female common Goldeneys can exhibit all orange bills like this one. To separate this bird from a female Barrow's Goldeneye, I looked at the bill's shape; it is quite long in relation to the duck's head size and similar in shape to those of the others in the flock. Barrow's Goldeneyes have particularly short bills, a feature that is enhanced by their steep foreheads. These birds all show the sloped forehead and peak over the eye that is consistent with Common Goldeneyes.

description:
Bufflehead (Bucefala albeola)

21 February 2015: Bufflehead (Bucefala albeola) is a native North American duck species that has no permanent range but is truly a migratory bird of this part of the world. Its wintering, migratory, and breeding range extends on the north from western Alaska to the Caribbean (Cuba in particular) and southcentral Mexico. Bufflehead breeding range is to the north in Alaska and in western and central Canada to the Great Lakes area and Hudson Bay. Its wintering range extends from the offshore islands of Alaska’s southcentral coast south to encompass most of the continental United States (except southern Florida where this species is entirely absent according to the range map in All About Birds) and on into Mexico where about three-quarters of the country is home to Bufflehead during its wintering flight. This observation was made at one of the two lakes at South Lakes Park in Denton, Texas. Because of its extensive mobile range throughout North America as indicated, Bufflehead is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. South Lakes Park is administered by the City of Denton, Texas.

Source: “Bufflehead,” All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, range map, photographs, description, resource links, accessed 1.4.16, https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Bufflehead/id

22 January 2016: While hiking at the Lewisville Lake Environmental Learning Area (LLELA) in Lewisville, Texas, we observed several Bufflehead (Bucephala albeola) pairs on the ponds and taking off upon our approach which are the images depicted in our posted observation. Bufflehead winters over most of North America in Mexico, United States (including Alaska) and Canada and migrates and breeds in Canada. It also winters in the Caribbean especially Cuba. Little 3 part behavior series

It was an overcast morning when I saw buffleheads out on the lake.  Seems they never come in close to shore.  The male seemed to be showing off for the female.  Thought he was going to dive but he didn't.  He just sat up tall in the water for a bit then settled back down.  She seemed impressed.
Photo 2:  Female Bufflehead Shows Her Wings Off
After he settled back down on the water, she raised up and flapped her wings.  
Photo 3:  Trouble In Bufflehead Paradise

description:
White Rock lake, Sunset Bay
Photo 1:
Male Bufflehead Swimming By

Buffleheads are unusual ducks.  They tend to stay far away from the shores but on this occasion they were a little closer.  Easy to spot with all that black and  white. This male swam past me as I stood on the pier.
Photo 2:
About To Dive

When the light hits the head just right, you can see a pretty iridescence of purple and green on a male bufflehead.  I got a quick glimpse of that right before he dived.
Photo 3:
Two Female Spectators
There were two female buffleheads nearby watching the male.  
Photo 4:
The Choice Is Made
All 3 buffles dived under the water.  These two came up together and swam off together.  Not sure where the other female  went.  Sometimes they can come up a longs ways from where they dive so it is easy to lose sight of them.

description:
White Rock lake, Sunset Bay
Photo 1:
Slamming On The Brakes
I captured a funny sequence of behaviors of bufflehead ducks.  This male was flying low over the water when he spotted a female and abruptly slammed on the brakes and came to a halt.
Photo 2:
Showing Off For The Lady
Now that he had the attention of the female bufflehead, the male went into his courtship dance.  This was really cool and something I'd  never seen before.
Photo 3:
Dog & Pony Show
The male did the funniest dance across the surface of the water as he showed off for the female.  She seemed appreciative. 
Photo 4:
Wham Bam!
This happened almost too fast for me to get a shot.  The male stopped his dance and jumped on top of the female and commenced mating.  His weight pushed her completely under the water.  Next thing I knew, they both were out of sight under the water.  Buffleheads are diving ducks but I don't know if they actually mate underwater.  Maybe.  When they came back up, at least 30 seconds later, they were much further away from me and constantly diving so the show seemed to be over.

description:
This seems to be a female Barrow's Goldeneye in breeding plumage.  I went there looking for it due to reports that it had been seen.  Several expert birders were there and confirmed the ID, though the female is very similar to the Common Goldeneye female (of which there were 8 or more.  The Barrow's has a shorter bill which is mostly pink or orange.  The Common's larger and mostly black bill is pretty evident (if you have enough zoom).  

I found it stayed with a couple CG females and one male CG a lot of the time, but it seemed to be the lead bird with the females most of the time.  

It seemed to do even more preening than the others.

The slight textbook size difference 2.1 versus 1.9 pounds seemed just noticeable.

So, anyways, the first time this species has been reported in Santa Cruz in 10 years or so.  

Fun stuff!  

Disclaimer:  I am not a bird expert, I just play one on T.V.  I only offer these morsels of information in case someone is dying to see this bird, now might be your chance.  It seems to stay pretty close to the trestle, usually withing a couple hundred feet upstream.

description: "Buffleheads are small diving ducks that exhibit strong sexual dimorphism. Males with breeding plumage are predominately black and white, with a black head and back that appears iridescent green and purple. They have a white underbelly and a distinguishing large white patch extending from the nape of the neck to the crown of the head. Males have blue-gray bills and pink webbed feet. Females are similar in plumage to male yearlings. They are grey on the bottom and brown on top with a white patch on the sides of the head. Both male yearlings and adult females have bills that are dark gray to black and legs and toes that are dark pink while webbed feet are brown. The ear patch of female buffleheads is more defined than the that of yearling males. The downy coats of hatchlings are black to dark grey with a white patched cheeks, throats, lower breasts, and bellies. (Gauthier, 1993; McKinney and McWilliams, 2005; Usai, 1999)     Buffleheads are native to North America. Their summer breeding range includes central Alaska and extends south to British Columbia and east to Saskatchewan. Isolated breeding populations can also be found throughout the northern United States and in Quebec. Their winter distribution is generally split into two populations, one on the east coast and the other on the west coast of North America."

description: Buffleheads are found throughout the United States, with a preferred habits being lakes, ponds and rivers; however, it will in salt water bays during the winter. These are small ducks and males and females both have unique features. The males have a large patch on the back of its head, with a dark back and white underside. Females are mostly brown but have a distinct white patch on its cheek. In this picture, you can see both male and female individuals. After mating females will lay a clutch of 8-10 eggs, and she will incubate them for about a month. Young are led to water only a couple days after hatching, but will be able to fly after 50-55 days. They are considered to be mostly secondary consumers feeding underwater on invertebrates, crustaceans, and mollusks. A potential predator could be Common Periwinkle snail, and a potential predator could be Bald Eagles. It could also compete with common Loons.

description: An adult male Common Goldeneye (Bucephala clangula) and an adult male Barrow's Goldeneye (Bucephala islandica), photographed at Shoreline Lake in Mojntain View, CA.  This shot offers a nice side-by-side comparison of these too closely related (and very similar) birds.  The Barrow's Goldeneye is the bird in the foreground, with the teardrop or comma-shaped cheek patch, the closed-off pattern of light-and-dark bars on the upper flanks with the dark spur at the shoulders, and the puffier mane of feathers at the back of the head.  In contrast, the Common Goldeneye has the round cheek patch, the lighter pattern on the flanks (lacking the dark bar across the bottom or the shoulder spur), and the more peaked head (no mane at the back).

description:
Bufflehead (Bucephala albeola)

Usual size: approx 13-14", with a wingspan of 20" +/-.

Other facts: Usually found in lakes, ponds, and rivers. Makes its nest in trees. One of the smallest ducks. Is a diver, not a dabbler, and predominately eats insects along with aquatic plants and fish eggs as well as snails.

Waterfowl/Birds seen in vicinity: Ring-billed gull (Larus delawarensis), approximately 18-20. Lake was partially frozen.

Day 1: This was the start of my year of the Bufflehead. I'd seen a couple in the area in previous years, but never at this site or in these numbers. It was surprising to find them in what was basically a retention pond in a suburban complex. It began with 2 pair. Surprisingly, they remained for quite a while, contented and hunting successfully. The number and composition of the group changed over time, but they all seemed to get along. Idk if they were part of various flocks, seeing the pond as safe because there were others present and moving on in their own time with members of their flock. Or were they part of a larger flock, exploring different parts of the area with a subset stopping here at various times?
I tried to check in on them frequently, and document how many birds there were as the group changed.
